evidence.claim: Bridger Valley Historic Byway follows paved roads through Fort Bridger, Urie and Lyman on the I-80 Business Loop.
evidence.quote: Bridger Valley Historic Byway, 13 miles of paved road that also serves as the I-80 Business Loop through the towns of Lyman, Urie, and Ft. Bridger.

evidence.claim: The Wyoming Transportation Commission adopted it into the state’s Scenic Byways and Backways Program.
evidence.quote: This appendix includes the twelve byways and five backways adopted by the Wyoming Transportation Commission into the Wyoming Scenic Byways and Backways Program.

evidence.claim: WYDOT describes that program as a way to combine travel with appreciation and protection of the state’s scenic, historic and cultural resources.
evidence.quote: promote and enhance tourism and the understanding and appreciation of the state’s heritage in concert with the preservation, protection and enhancement of the state’s scenic, historic and cultural resources.

evidence.claim: Jim Bridger and Louis Vasquez established a trading post here to serve travelers heading west.
evidence.quote: Fort Bridger was established in 1843 by Jim Bridger and Louis Vasquez. It served as a trading post for those who were traveling westward along the Oregon Trail

evidence.claim: Its blacksmith shop offered travelers a service even when supplies and prices drew complaints.
evidence.quote: Most visitors complained about insufficient supplies and it being overpriced. They did, however, have a blacksmith's shop that many travelers took advantage of.

evidence.claim: The valley subsequently carried the Pony Express, transcontinental railroad and Lincoln Highway.
evidence.quote: For the next century, the region served as a crossroads for the "California/Oregon Trail, the Mormon Trail, the Pony Express Route, the Transcontinental Railroad, and the Lincoln Highway.

evidence.claim: In 1925, the Black and Orange Cabins opened beside the fort to accommodate automobile travelers on the Lincoln Highway.
evidence.quote: The Black and Orange Cabins are a motel constructed next to Fort Bridger in southwest Wyoming. The cabins were originally constructed in 1925 along the Lincoln Highway, giving automobile tourist lodging accommodations while travelling through Wyoming.

evidence.claim: Traveling east through the valley, the business loop connects Fort Bridger, Urie and Lyman.
evidence.quote: the I-80 Business Loop through the towns of Lyman, Urie, and Ft. Bridger.

evidence.claim: At Urie, a spur runs south to Mountain View; another spur leads north to the old railroad town of Carter.
evidence.quote: A 2 ½ mile spur from Urie to the 28 south brings travelers to the town of Mountain View, Wyoming; and a 7 mile spur to the north delivers visitors to the old railroad town of Carter, Wyoming.

evidence.claim: The trading post at Fort Bridger is a reconstruction.
evidence.quote: Jim Bridger’s trading post is reconstructed

evidence.claim: Jim Bridger and Louis Vasquez established the original post, which became a resupply point for wagon trains on the Oregon, California and Mormon trails.
evidence.quote: The post was established by the mountain man Jim Bridger, after whom it is named, and Louis Vasquez.

evidence.claim: In an 1843 letter to Pierre Chouteau Jr., Bridger described a blacksmith shop and a supply of iron on the emigrants’ road.
evidence.quote: In December 1843, Bridger wrote to Pierre Chouteau Jr., "I have established a small fort, with a blacksmith shop and a supply of iron in the road of emigrants on Black Fork of Green River

evidence.claim: The U.S. Army established a military post here in 1858 and finally closed it in 1890.
evidence.quote: The US Army established a military post here in 1858 during the Utah War, until it was finally closed in 1890.

evidence.claim: The old Pony Express barn and Mormon protective wall survive at the historic fort.
evidence.quote: The historical Fort Bridger has several interesting old buildings still standing: the old Pony Express barn and the Mormon protective wall.

evidence.quote: It became a vital resupply point for wagon trains on the Oregon, California, and Mormon Trails.

evidence.claim: The Black and Orange Cabins beside Fort Bridger served a later generation of travelers: motorists on the Lincoln Highway.
evidence.quote: The Black and Orange Cabins are a motel constructed next to Fort Bridger in southwest Wyoming. The cabins were originally constructed in 1925 along the Lincoln Highway, giving automobile tourist lodging accommodations while travelling through Wyoming.

evidence.claim: Built in 1925, the tourist lodging operated until 1936.
evidence.quote: The site was active from 1925 until 1936.

evidence.claim: The property then remained essentially abandoned from 1948 to 1996.
evidence.quote: The site remained essentially abandoned from 1948 until 1996.

evidence.claim: The Fort Bridger Historical Society bought it in 1996 and donated it to the state.
evidence.quote: In 1996, the site was purchased by the Fort Bridger Historical Society and was then donated to the state

evidence.claim: Wyoming began restoring the cabins in 2007, stabilizing foundations and repairing chimneys and roofs.
evidence.quote: The State of Wyoming began an extensive restoration project in 2007, including foundation stabilization of the cabins, and foundation, chimney, and roof repairs.

evidence.claim: That round of restoration ended in June 2009.
evidence.quote: This round of restoration was completed in June 2009.

evidence.claim: Lyman is one of the towns on the byway’s I-80 Business Loop.
evidence.quote: the I-80 Business Loop through the towns of Lyman, Urie, and Ft. Bridger.

evidence.claim: It also has a connection to astronomy: the privately owned Mountain Skies Observatory is located here and used by the Bridger Valley Astronomical Society.
evidence.quote: Mountain Skies Observatory  is a privately owned astronomical observatory located in Lyman, Wyoming, USA. It is one of the largest observatories in the region and is used frequently by the Bridger Valley Astronomical Society.

evidence.claim: The site and remaining buildings passed to Wyoming’s Historical Landmark Commission in 1928.
evidence.quote: On June 27, 1928, the site of the fort, and remaining buildings, were sold to the Historical Landmark Commission of Wyoming.

evidence.claim: A sale in 1941 brought new ownership, but the cabins likely never reopened.
evidence.quote: It was sold to a new owner in 1941, but was likely never again opened.

flags: The cache gives little terrain or road-character detail beyond a paved business loop; the overview is shorter than the target. No driving time, curves or mountain views have been inferred.
Mileage differs by scope: WYDOT gives 13 miles plus spurs, the valley article approximately 20 miles, and material 18.2 mapped miles. Omitted pending corridor review.

Fort founding date conflicts: the town article says 1842 in its lead and 1843 in its history; the fort article says 1842 and the valley article 1843. Omitted founding year; the dated 1843 letter is retained as a separate fact.
Lyman is deliberately short: the observatory cache is brief and provides no public-access evidence. Private ownership is explicit.
Strip miles put Urie before Fort Bridger despite its location east of the fort; retained moments follow geographic west-to-east order. Confirm strip-map geometry.
No current site-manager cache confirms visitor access at the fort or restored cabins; the story makes no promise of access.
